title: Raksha Bandhan
hookLine: a Hindu festival where sisters tie a thread on brothers' wrists, a bond of protection

lines: A LAMP, A SWEET, A THREAD.
cards: A plate on a small tray: a little lamp, a pinch of red powder, a few grains of rice, a sweet, and a bright thread with a flower of tinsel in the middle. A sister holds it.
Her brother sits in front of her, wrist out, a little embarrassed, a little pleased. She marks his forehead, ties the thread, feeds him the sweet. He gives her a gift and a promise.
Hindu families who keep the festival, in India and far beyond, share scenes like this one day each year.

teach.b: First, the name. Raksha means protection, and bandhan means a tie, a bond: the bond of protection. The thread itself is usually called a rakhi.
The sister ties it and prays for her brother's wellbeing, and the brother promises to stand by her. Second, the stories behind it. Hindus tell more than one.
One, told in the Puranas, the old story collections, has the goddess Indrani tying a protective thread on the wrist of her husband Indra, king of the gods, before a battle.
Another, a story people tell about the Mahabharata, has Draupadi tearing a strip from her sari to bind a cut on Krishna's finger, and Krishna, years later, protecting her in her hour of need.
These are tradition's stories, told in more than one version, and people tell them for what they mean more than as history. Third, what the thread does. A rakhi is light.
It snaps easily. It frays. Nobody is protected by its strength.
The protection lives in what it stands for: someone remembered you, someone promised. The thread is the small visible end of a large invisible bond.
Fourth, how wide it reaches. Some families tie rakhis between cousins, and between friends who have chosen to be like brother and sister.
Some sisters tie them on sisters. Some people send them by mail across oceans. The heart of the day isn't who ties it.
It's the promise: I'm on your side, and I'm not going anywhere. This one ties love to a wrist, where it can be seen all day.

how: On Raksha Bandhan, Hindu sisters tie a rakhi on their brothers' wrists, mark their foreheads and offer sweets, and brothers give gifts and promise their protection; some families also include cousins and close friends.

o: a wedding ritual that ties the bride and groom together
a festival of lights honoring the goddess of wealth
the bond of protection: a thread a sister ties on a brother

games.q: what's inside the thread — tap the pairs.
p: tied a thread on Indra's wrist
bound a cut on Krishna's finger

s: the rakhi protects because the thread is strong
it snaps easily; the protection lives in the promise it stands for.
raksha bandhan means the bond of protection
raksha, protection; bandhan, a tie or bond.
only brothers and sisters by birth can tie a rakhi
some families tie them between cousins and between friends who are like family.

games.q: in the story people tell, Krishna has cut his finger and it's bleeding. Draupadi is standing beside him. what does she do?
o: tear a strip from her sari and bind the cut.
pray for him from a distance.
games.why: she tears a strip from her sari and ties it on. in the story, Krishna later protects her: a thread given, a promise kept.

practice: Rest your hands palms up and feel the inside of your wrist, where a thread would go, then bring to mind someone who has stood by you, a sibling, a cousin, a friend, anyone who has been family to you, and remember a moment they kept you safe.
Hold both of you in mind, as if one thread ran between your wrists, and if you pray, ask for their protection in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Raksha Bandhan. The bond of protection, a Hindu festival when a sister ties a thread on her brother's wrist and he promises to stand by her. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Hindi: raksha, protection; bandhan, a tie or bond.

carryVoice: Your line: the thread. The thread is thin; the promise is what holds. That's day eight hundred seventy-six.
